I used to work as a librarian in a small, quirky town with a population of around 5,000 people. The town was nestled in the rolling hills of rural England, and it had a way of making you feel at home. Every time a new person moved in, the locals would make it a point to introduce themselves with a friendly "Welcome to Willowdale!" and a wedding-like assortment of baked goods.

As a librarian, I had the pleasure of being surrounded by books all day, every day. The musty smell of old pages and the gentle rustle of the whispering patrons are experiences you don't get to have many places. I loved it, and I thought it was the most peaceful thing I'd ever found.

We had a peculiar patron, a retired professor who claimed to have written a novel. He'd visit the library at least thrice a week, insisting we'd helped him find the exact words he needed for his book. Since it took him an eternity to finish his manuscript – ten years, at least – it became more a ritual than anything else. In reality, I suspected his answer was basically scribbled in the margins of the same county history texts we'd had on the shelves since the '50s.

Local students would come to our library often, flaunting modest photography skills or the occasional watercolor display of field responses.
